content: At the time of presentation or when a patient’s CD4 count falls below the eligibility threshold, antiretroviral therapy (ART) is initiated. Individuals presenting with WHO stage 3 or 4 conditions are started on ART immediately. Between 2004 and 2011, the rate of ART initiation was approximately five per year, which decreased to two per year after 2011. Among those deemed eligible for ART, 75% link to care and begin treatment after a delay ranging from immediate initiation to up to four months. In 2015, mortality rates among individuals on ART were as follows: for those on ART for less than six months, the mortality rate was 21 per 1,000 person-years (PYs); for those on ART for six months or more, the rate was 11 per 1,000 PYs. However, in certain subpopulations, mortality rates were higher, such as 58 per 1,000 PYs for those on ART for less than six months and 14 per 1,000 PYs for those on ART for six months or more. Additionally, 25% of individuals lost to follow-up spontaneously returned to care within two years, while 50% returned after developing an opportunistic infection (OI). Among those disengaging from ART, 25% were permanently lost, while 75% resumed treatment later. Between 2004 and 2015, HIV-related deaths per 1,000 HIV-positive adults declined significantly in several countries due to ART scale-up: by 66% in Rwanda, 48% in Kenya, 69% in Malawi, and 44% in South Africa. However, a substantial proportion of HIV-related deaths occurred among individuals who had not initiated ART. It is estimated that 20–30% of HIV deaths occurred among undiagnosed individuals, and 25–45% occurred among those who were either never diagnosed or never linked to care. These patterns align with independent empirical findings. Projections indicate that, without improvements in diagnosis, linkage to care, and ART initiation, 30–50% of HIV-related deaths in the coming decade will occur among individuals who never started ART. Conversely, adults stable on ART for more than six months are expected to comprise the largest share of HIV-positive adults (approximately 60%) but contribute a much smaller proportion of HIV-related deaths (17–30%) due to their significantly lower mortality rates (7–15 per 1,000 PYs). Mathematical models for Kenya, Malawi, and South Africa suggest that immediate ART initiation for all patients presenting for HIV care could reduce HIV-related mortality by 6–15% over the next decade compared to current guidelines, which recommend initiation at CD4 counts below 500. This reduction is attributed to preventing losses during the pre-ART care stage. Immediate ART initiation also has the potential to reduce HIV transmission over the long term. The effectiveness of immediate ART initiation was demonstrated in the RapIT trial in Johannesburg, where 98% of eligible patients initiated ART within 90 days when same-day ART initiation was offered, compared to 72% under standard procedures. Retention in care and viral suppression rates after six months were similar between the two groups. A combination of interventions, including improved HIV testing, linkage to care, retention on ART, and immediate ART eligibility, is projected to generate greater health gains than any single intervention. Such a comprehensive approach is likely to avert disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) cost-effectively. Strengthening the HIV care cascade, including immediate ART initiation, could maximize health benefits in resource-limited settings. Understanding the sources of HIV mortality in settings with widespread ART availability is critical for identifying effective interventions to further reduce mortality and morbidity. As ART coverage increases, most HIV-positive adults are on treatment, but mortality rates remain higher among those not actively engaged in care. Interventions focused on diagnosing, linking, and retaining patients in care may yield greater health benefits than those aimed at improving care for patients already stable on ART. In conclusion, immediate ART initiation, irrespective of CD4 count, offers pragmatic benefits by reducing pre-ART losses and improving retention in care. These findings highlight the importance of prioritizing interventions that address gaps in the HIV care cascade to achieve substantial and cost-effective health gains.
